alternative: Keep the state in a parent-owned container and pass it down explicitly - a Laminar Var/Signal, a case class of callbacks, or a child render function - and let the reactive graph propagate changes; use ScalaFX/JavaFX ToggleGroup when a toolkit group object is what is actually needed, rather than emulating an ambient component tree with givens or dynamic scope.
idiom_name: no component tree and no per-instance implicit scope: explicit parameters or a framework state container
implementation_notes: Scala has no component tree, and its contextual abstractions do not model this pattern: Scala 3 givens and implicit parameters are resolved lexically from the definition and use site - the contextual-abstractions chapter frames them as a way of passing arguments without repeating them, effectively a service/configuration channel - not per parent instance, so a given cannot carry per-widget state safely. The old dynamic-scope workaround (scala.util.DynamicVariable) is thread-local, invisible in types and has no re-render story, which is why it never became an idiom. Front-end Scala keeps composition explicit: a Laminar parent owns a Var/Signal and passes values or child render functions down, and the reactive graph - not an ambient parent object - propagates changes.
pitfalls: A given or implicit val is resolved once per lexical scope, not per parent instance, so several widgets on a page would silently share one value.
DynamicVariable is thread-local and leaks across asynchronous boundaries (Futures, actors) unless carefully restored, so it cannot carry UI state.
JavaFX-based Scala gets a real group object (ToggleGroup) only inside that toolkit; Scala itself supplies no grouping primitive to fall back on.
Emulating the channel with a global mutable object looks like the pattern but breaks the moment two instances exist on the same screen.
